title: Submarines and underwater vehicles
description: Density and Archimedes, neutral buoyancy, ballast tanks, pressure, hulls, propulsion, stability, sensors and depth control with PID — up to the full budget of an ROV.

sub-01-arquimedes.title: Density and Archimedes' principle
sub-01-arquimedes.theory:
# Why does a steel ship float?

A steel bolt sinks; a 100 000-tonne steel ship floats. The difference is the **average density**:

```
density = mass / volume      (kg/m³)
```

- fresh water: **1 000 kg/m³** (1 litre = 1 kg)
- sea water: **~1 025 kg/m³**
- steel: ~7 850 kg/m³; wood: 500–800 kg/m³

The ship is steel **plus a lot of air** inside: the total mass divided by the total volume gives less than that of water.

## Archimedes' principle

Every body immersed in a liquid receives an upward force, the **buoyancy**, equal to the **weight of the liquid it displaces**:

```
buoyancy = ρ_water × g × V_displaced
```

A 20 L hull fully submerged in fresh water displaces 20 kg of water: buoyancy = 1 000 × 9.81 × 0.020 = **196.2 N**.

## Does it sink, float or stay put?

Compare the buoyancy with the **weight** (m × g):

- **buoyancy > weight** → the net force is upwards: the body **rises** and floats with part of it out of the water (displacing only what is needed);
- **buoyancy < weight** → it **sinks**;
- **buoyancy = weight** → **neutral buoyancy**: it stays where it is placed.

Or, the quick way: if the **average density** is less than that of water, it floats.

## The simulator model

The hull is a horizontal cylinder (length = 6 diameters). The simulator adds up weight, buoyancy (which decreases as the hull leaves the water), water drag and the "added mass" of water the hull has to push in order to move.
sub-01-arquimedes.task: This 20 L hull has 21 kg and **sinks**. Change the hull's **volume** or **mass** so that it **floats** (positive buoyancy balance and ending at the surface).
hints: Calculate the average density: 21 kg / 20 L = 1.05 kg/L. Greater than fresh water (1 kg/L)…
A larger hull displaces more water; a lighter one weighs less. Either one solves it.

questions.prompt: What is the buoyancy on a **20 L** hull fully submerged in **fresh water**? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
What is the average density of a **21 kg** ROV with a volume of **20 L**?
questions.explanation: 21 kg / 0.020 m³ = 1 050 kg/m³ — denser than fresh water, so it sinks.

questions.prompt: Why does a steel ship float, if steel is ~8 times denser than water?
options: Because the hull paint is waterproof
Because, counting the air inside, the ship's average density is less than that of water
Because the engine pushes it up
Because salt water is denser than steel
questions.explanation: The hull displaces an enormous volume of water; the total mass (steel + air + cargo) divided by that volume gives less than 1 025 kg/m³.

goals: Positive buoyancy balance (buoyancy greater than weight)
Ends up floating at the surface

sub-02-flutuabilidade-neutra.title: Neutral buoyancy: neither rising nor sinking
sub-02-flutuabilidade-neutra.theory:
# The ideal state of a submarine

A submarine that **rises** by itself has to spend energy to stay down; one that **sinks** by itself spends energy not to go under. The ideal is **neutral buoyancy**: buoyancy = weight, and the vehicle stays still at the depth where it is, like a fish.

## Fine tuning with fixed ballast

In practice the hull is designed **a little light** and then small lead weights (**fixed ballast** or **trim**) are added until the balance is close to zero. Lead is good for this: very dense (11 340 kg/m³), it gives a lot of mass in a small space.

```
missing mass = ρ_water × V − current mass
```

A 10 L, 9.6 kg ROV in fresh water needs 10 − 9.6 = **0.4 kg** of ballast.

## Fresh vs salt

Sea water is ~2.5% denser: the same hull receives **more buoyancy** in the sea. A submarine that is neutral in a river **rises** when it enters the sea, and needs more ballast. (Ships too: there are marks on the hull — the "Plimsoll line" — for each type of water.)

## In the simulator

The vehicle starts at a depth of **5 m**. If it is neutral, it stays there. The trim lead sits inside the hull (it adds mass, not volume).
sub-02-flutuabilidade-neutra.task: This ROV will work **in the sea**. With 19.5 kg in 20 L it rises to the surface. Choose the right **water** and add **lead** until it is **neutral** (balance between −0.3 and +0.3 N), staying near 5 m.
sub-02-flutuabilidade-neutra.safety: To test a model submarine or a real ROV, use a **swimming pool or shallow tank**, never rivers or the sea alone, and always with an adult nearby. Batteries and electronics stay **sealed**; nothing plugged into the mains near the water.
hints: In the sea, 20 L of water weigh 20 × 1.025 = 20.5 kg.
How much is missing from 19.5 kg to 20.5 kg? Convert to grams.

questions.prompt: A **10 L** ROV with **9.6 kg** will dive in **fresh water**. How many grams of lead make it neutral (ignoring the volume of the lead)?
questions.explanation: It displaces 10 kg of fresh water; 10 − 9.6 = 0.4 kg = 400 g are missing.

questions.prompt: A neutral submarine in a river moves into the sea. What happens?
options: It sinks, because salt water is heavier
It rises, because sea water is denser and gives more buoyancy
questions.explanation: Same displaced volume, denser water: the buoyancy increases ~2.5% and the balance becomes positive.

questions.prompt: Why is neutral buoyancy desirable in an underwater vehicle?
options: Because it does not need to spend energy just to hold its depth
questions.explanation: With buoyancy = weight, the thrusters only work to move the vehicle, and the batteries last longer.

goals: Stays between 4 and 6 m of depth

sub-03-lastro.title: Ballast tanks: diving and coming back
sub-03-lastro.theory:
# Changing weight without changing size

A submarine has to **go down** and then **come up**. Since the hull volume does not change, it changes its **mass**: it fills **ballast tanks** with sea water to sink and empties them to rise.

- **Flood** (open the top and bottom valves): water comes in, the submarine gets heavier → it **descends**.
- **Blow** (send compressed air into the tank): the air pushes the water out through the bottom, the submarine gets lighter → it **rises**.

The tanks' volume is **inside the hull envelope**, so it does not change the buoyancy, only the weight.

## How much to flood?

```
balance = ρ × g × V_hull − (m_hull + ρ × V_tank × fill) × g
```

To be neutral, the tank water must make up exactly what is missing. A 20 L, 19 kg hull in fresh water needs 1 kg of water: in a 3 L tank, that is **1/3 full (33%)**.

## Real submarines

Large submarines have **main tanks** (only completely full or empty, to submerge and surface) and smaller **compensating and trim tanks**, pumped little by little for fine adjustment. In an emergency, the main tanks are blown all at once: the submarine rises very fast ("emergency blow").

## In the simulator

The tank starts with the chosen fill level; at the moment "empty ballast at" the compressed air expels the water in ~4 s. The bottom is at 20 m.
sub-03-lastro.task: Make the submarine **go down to at least 15 m** and then **come back to the surface by itself** before the 120 s run out. Choose how much to **flood the ballast** and **when to blow it**.
hints: With 20% ballast it still floats. To sink fast, flood a lot more.
It takes some time to go down and as much to come up. Blow the ballast roughly halfway through the time.

questions.prompt: **20 L** hull, **19 kg** mass, **3 L** ballast tank, in fresh water. What percentage of the tank must be full for the submarine to be **neutral**?
questions.explanation: 20 − 19 = 1 kg = 1 L of water is missing. 1 L / 3 L = 33.3%.

questions.prompt: To rise, the submarine…
options: opens the tanks to let more water in
blows compressed air into the tanks, expelling the water
increases the size of the hull
heats the water in the tanks
questions.explanation: The compressed air pushes the water out: less mass with the same volume = positive balance.

questions.prompt: Why does flooding the ballast tank **not** change the buoyancy?
options: Because the tank is already inside the hull volume: the displaced volume is the same
Because the water in the tank has no weight
Because buoyancy only depends on depth
It does change, the buoyancy doubles
questions.explanation: Buoyancy depends on the external displaced volume. The water only replaces the air inside the tank: it increases the weight, not the volume.

goals: Reaches at least 15 m of depth
Returns to the surface at the end

sub-04-pressao.title: Pressure and depth
sub-04-pressao.theory:
# Every 10 m, 1 more bar

The pressure underwater is the weight of the column of water above each square metre, **plus** the pressure of the atmosphere:

```
P = P0 + ρ × g × h
```

- P0 = 101 325 Pa ≈ 1 bar (the air above the water)
- ρ × g × h: the water pressure ("gauge")

In fresh water, ρ × g = 9 810 Pa per metre: every **~10 m** the pressure increases by **~1 bar**. At 30 m in the sea the absolute pressure is already **~4 bar** — four times that at the surface.

## The hull withstands the difference

Inside the hull the air is at ~1 atm. The hull has to resist the **difference** between outside and inside: the gauge pressure. If it exceeds the hull's limit, it **collapses** (implodes) — all at once, in milliseconds.

```
collapse depth = strength / (ρ × g)
```

A 5 bar hull in fresh water withstands down to 5 × 10^5 / 9 810 ≈ **51 m**.

## Safety factor

Engineers never design at the limit: they use a **safety factor** (SF):

```
SF = hull strength / maximum working pressure
```

Too low an SF is dangerous (defective material, fatigue, calculation error); too high an SF makes the hull heavy and expensive. For underwater equipment something between 1.25 and 2 is common (crewed submarines use more).

## In the simulator

The ballast is full: the vehicle sinks to the bottom, at 40 m, in the sea. The dashed red line shows where the hull collapses.
sub-04-pressao.task: This hull only withstands 3 bar and **implodes** before reaching the bottom, at 40 m in the sea. Choose the **hull strength** to reach the bottom intact, with a **safety factor between 1.25 and 2** (safe, but without overdoing weight and cost).
sub-04-pressao.safety: Pressure hulls store a lot of energy. Test hulls and vessels with **water** (hydrostatic test), never with compressed air: water barely compresses, so if something gives way there is no explosion. Never take a camera or equipment deeper than the depth indicated by the manufacturer.
hints: Calculate the gauge pressure at the bottom: 1 025 × 9.81 × 40 ≈ 4 bar.
SF = strength / pressure at the bottom. For an SF between 1.25 and 2, the strength is between ~5 and ~8 bar.

questions.prompt: What is the **absolute** pressure at **30 m** depth in the sea? (ρ = 1 025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², P0 = 101 325 Pa) Answer in bar.
A hull that resists a **5 bar** pressure difference can go down to what depth in **fresh water**?
What does a submarine's hull have to withstand?
options: Only the absolute pressure of the water
The difference between the water pressure outside and the air pressure inside
Only the weight of the water above the submarine
Nothing, the water pushes equally in all directions
questions.explanation: Inside there is ~1 atm; outside, P0 + ρgh. The hull holds the difference, ρgh (the gauge pressure).

goals: Reaches the bottom (39 m or more)

sub-05-casco-materiais.title: Hull design and materials
sub-05-casco-materiais.theory:
# The shape that withstands pressure

Pressure pushes **equally in all directions**. The shape that best resists this is the **sphere**: the whole wall works under equal compression. That is why bathyscaphes and deep submersibles have a **spherical** cabin. The **cylinder** with rounded end caps is the best compromise for a long vehicle (room for motor, battery, crew).

## Wall stress

For a thin-walled cylinder (radius r, thickness t) under pressure P, the wall stress ("hoop" stress) is:

```
σ = P × r / t
```

With P = 3 MPa (~300 m), r = 0.1 m and t = 5 mm: σ = 3 × 0.1 / 0.005 = **60 MPa** — easy for aluminium (it resists ~250 MPa), but be careful with the next item.

## Buckling: the danger of thin hulls

Under **external** pressure, a thin hull does not fail because the material "bursts": it **buckles** — it loses its round shape and crumples suddenly, long before the breaking stress. The solution is to use **stiffening rings** (frames) inside or thicker walls. Any ovalisation (a dented hull) greatly worsens the strength.

## Materials

- **Acrylic (PMMA)**: transparent, great for camera domes and shallow ROVs; fragile against impacts and scratches.
- **Aluminium (6061-T6)**: light, easy to machine; needs corrosion protection in the sea (anodising, sacrificial anodes).
- **High-strength steel (HY-80/HY-100)**: military submarines; heavy, but tough and weldable.
- **Titanium**: very high strength per weight and does not corrode; expensive. Used in deep-sea vehicles.
- **Carbon-fibre composites**: light, but hard to inspect; internal damage and fatigue under pressure cycles have caused catastrophic failures.
- **Syntactic foam**: hollow glass microspheres in resin; gives **buoyancy** at great depths without being crushed (ordinary foam gets crushed).

## Sealing

Hulls open and close with **O-rings** in grooves; cables pass through **watertight connectors** (penetrators). Most leaks in amateur projects come from poor sealing, not a weak hull.

questions.prompt: Why do deep submersibles have a **spherical** cabin?
options: Because the sphere distributes the pressure equally over the whole wall, resisting better with less material
Because the sphere is more hydrodynamic
questions.explanation: In a sphere the whole wall is compressed equally; there are no weak points of shape.

questions.prompt: Calculate the wall stress of a cylinder with **P = 3 MPa**, radius **0.1 m** and thickness **5 mm** (σ = P × r / t). Answer in MPa.
A thin cylindrical hull under **external** pressure usually fails by…
options: buckling: it loses its round shape and crumples suddenly, before the breaking stress
questions.explanation: Under compression, thin structures are unstable. Stiffening rings and thicker walls prevent buckling.

questions.prompt: To provide buoyancy to an ROV working at **3 000 m**, you use…
options: syntactic foam (hollow glass microspheres in resin)
questions.explanation: Ordinary foams and bottles are crushed by the pressure; syntactic foam resists and stays light.

questions.prompt: Why are hulls and tanks tested with **water** (hydrostatic test) and not with air?
options: Because water barely compresses: it stores little energy and, if something gives way, there is no explosion
Because air does not make pressure
questions.explanation: Compressed gas stores a lot of energy and releases it all at once in a failure; water practically does not.

sub-06-propulsao-arrasto.title: Propulsion and drag
sub-06-propulsao-arrasto.theory:
# Pushing water is expensive

Water is ~800 times denser than air, so the drag underwater is enormous. The formula is the same as for air:

```
F_drag = ½ × ρ × v² × Cd × A
```

At **cruising speed** the thruster pushes exactly the drag:

```
v = √( 2 × F / (ρ × Cd × A) )
```

## Shape: Cd

- **Torpedo** (rounded nose and tapering tail): Cd ≈ 0.1 — the water slides by and closes behind.
- **Flat-ended cylinder**: Cd ≈ 0.85 — the front hits the water and a swirl forms behind.
- **Open box** (frame ROV): Cd ≈ 1.05 — practical for carrying cameras, arms and lights, but slow.

## Power goes with the cube

Useful power = force × speed. Since force grows with v², power grows with **v³**: doubling the speed costs **8 times** more power. That is why submarines move slowly (and ROVs even more so).

```
P_useful = F × v
P_battery ≈ P_useful / η     (η ≈ 0.4 combining motor and propeller)
```

## In the simulator

The forward thruster pushes with the chosen force; the frontal area is that of the hull's circle (a 20 L cylinder has a diameter of 16 cm). The power shown is what leaves the battery, at 40% efficiency.
sub-06-propulsao-arrasto.task: This box-shaped ROV moves at under 1 m/s. Choose the **shape** and the **thruster force** to cruise at **at least 1.5 m/s** using **at most 40 W** from the battery.
sub-06-propulsao-arrasto.safety: Propellers and thrusters have sharp blades that spin fast: use **guards** ("kort nozzle" or mesh) and never power the motors with someone holding the vehicle near the propellers. Switch off the power before touching anything.
hints: With the box, to reach 1.5 m/s you would need ~24 N and ~90 W. Change the shape.
With the torpedo, a few newtons are enough.

questions.prompt: An ROV cruises at **2 m/s** with **20 N** of drag. What is the thruster's useful power?
questions.explanation: P = F × v = 20 × 2 = 40 W (more would leave the battery, because of the efficiency).

questions.prompt: If the submarine doubles its speed, the required power…
questions.explanation: F grows with v² and P = F × v, so P grows with v³: 2³ = 8.

questions.prompt: Why does the torpedo shape have so much less drag than a box?
options: Because the water slides along the rounded front and closes behind the tapered tail, without big swirls
questions.explanation: Almost all the drag of blunt shapes comes from the low-pressure wake behind them; the tapered tail avoids the wake.

goals: Cruising speed of at least 1.5 m/s
Battery power of at most 40 W

sub-07-estabilidade.title: Stability: centre of gravity vs centre of buoyancy
sub-07-estabilidade.theory:
# Two points again

As with rockets, a submarine's stability depends on two points:

- **Centre of gravity (CG)**: where the weight acts.
- **Centre of buoyancy (CB)**: the centre of the displaced volume, where the buoyancy acts.

Submerged, the CB stays put (it is the geometric centre of the hull). If the vehicle tilts and the **CG is below the CB**, weight and buoyancy form a **couple that rights it**, like a **roly-poly toy**. If the CG is **above**, the couple makes it **flip upside down**.

## The BG distance

```
righting moment = weight × BG × sin(angle)
```

BG is the vertical distance between the CB and the CG. More BG = it returns faster and rocks less. In small ROVs, a BG of 1 to 5 cm is common.

## How to lower the CG

- Put what is **heavy at the bottom**: batteries, lead in the **keel**.
- Put what is **light (floats, foam) on top**.
- Moving lead from the centre to the keel **does not change the buoyancy balance**, only the stability.

## What about ships?

At the surface it is different: when the ship heels, the shape of the submerged volume changes and the CB **shifts sideways**. The point that matters is the **metacentre (M)**: the ship is stable if the CG is below M — even if it is above the CB. Submerged, this "help" disappears: only CG below CB counts.

## In the simulator

The hull's centre of mass (structure, electronics) is 0.5 cm **above** the centre. The lead "in the centre" is at the height of the CB; the one "in the keel" is at the bottom of the hull. In the drawing: blue dot = CB, orange = CG (displacement exaggerated 3×).
sub-07-estabilidade.task: This ROV is neutral, but it **flips over**: the CG is above the CB. Redistribute the **lead** to put the CG **at least 1 cm below** the CB, keeping **neutral buoyancy**.
hints: Lead in the centre does not help stability. Move it to the keel.
If the total amount of lead does not change, the buoyancy balance stays at zero.

questions.prompt: An ROV weighing **200 N** has **BG = 2 cm**. What is the righting moment when it tilts **30°**? (sin 30° = 0.5)
For a **submerged** vehicle to be stable, the CG must be…
options: exactly at the centre of buoyancy
ahead of the centre of buoyancy
questions.explanation: With the CG at the bottom, weight and buoyancy form a couple that rights the vehicle (roly-poly effect).

questions.prompt: Why can a ship at the surface be stable even with the CG **above** the CB?
options: Because, when it heels, the submerged part changes shape and the CB shifts sideways (what counts is the metacentre)
It cannot; every ship has its CG below the CB
questions.explanation: The sideways shift of the CB creates a righting couple as long as the CG is below the metacentre M.

goals: CG at least 1 cm below the centre of buoyancy

sub-08-sensores-navegacao.title: Sensors and navigation: sonar, pressure and IMU
sub-08-sensores-navegacao.theory:
# Navigating in the dark

Underwater there is **no GPS**: radio waves (and light) are absorbed within a few metres. An underwater vehicle combines several sensors to know where it is.

## Pressure sensor: the depth

Since P = P0 + ρ × g × h, measuring the pressure is enough to know the depth:

```
h = (P − P0) / (ρ × g)
```

It is the most precise and cheapest sensor on the vehicle (some measure centimetres). It is what feeds the depth control.

## Sonar: seeing with sound

Sound travels well in water, at **~1 500 m/s** (4.4× faster than in air). A **sonar** emits a pulse and measures the time until the echo returns:

```
distance = speed of sound × time / 2
```

(divided by 2 because the sound goes **and comes back**). Echo sounders measure the distance to the bottom; side-scan sonars draw images of the seabed; imaging sonars show obstacles ahead.

## IMU: accelerometers and gyroscopes

The **IMU** (inertial measurement unit) measures accelerations and rotations. Integrating the acceleration once gives velocity; integrating again, position — this is **dead reckoning**. The problem: any small acceleration error is integrated **twice**, and the position error grows with the **square of time**. On its own, a cheap IMU gets lost within minutes.

## Putting it all together

- **DVL** (Doppler Velocity Log): measures the speed relative to the bottom by the Doppler effect of sound — much better than integrating accelerations.
- **Compass/magnetometer**: heading (disturbed by motors and metals).
- **Acoustic beacons (USBL/LBL)**: a ship at the surface (which has GPS) measures the vehicle's position by sound.
- **Kalman filter**: an algorithm that fuses all the sensors, trusting more whichever is most accurate at each moment.
sub-08-sensores-navegacao.safety: Powerful sonars can disturb and harm marine animals. In real projects, follow the environmental rules of the region and prefer low-power sensors.

questions.prompt: An echo sounder hears the echo from the bottom **0.04 s** after emitting the pulse. With sound at **1 500 m/s**, what is the distance to the bottom?
questions.explanation: 1 500 × 0.04 / 2 = 30 m (the sound goes and comes back).

questions.prompt: The pressure sensor of an ROV in **fresh water** reads **2.5 bar absolute**. What is the depth? (P0 = 101 325 Pa, g = 9.81 m/s²)
Why does GPS not work underwater?
options: Because the satellites do not pass over the sea
Because water absorbs radio waves within a few centimetres to metres
Because the pressure breaks the antenna
questions.explanation: Water (especially salt water, which is conductive) absorbs radio waves. That is why sound is used to communicate and position.

questions.prompt: Navigating with the IMU alone (integrating the acceleration twice), the position error…
options: grows with the square of time
questions.explanation: A constant acceleration error becomes a position error of ½·a·t²: it grows with t². That is why the IMU is combined with DVL, beacons and Kalman.

questions.prompt: Why do submarines use **sound** (sonar) instead of light or radar to "see"?
options: Because sound travels far in water, while light and radio are absorbed quickly
Because sound is faster than light in water
questions.explanation: Light reaches tens of metres in clear water; sound, kilometres.

sub-09-controle-pid.title: Depth control with PID
sub-09-controle-pid.theory:
# Holding the depth by itself

No vehicle is perfectly neutral: the water changes density, the load changes, the batteries heat up. A **controller** reads the pressure sensor (the depth) and commands the **vertical thruster** to hold the **target depth**.

## The error

```
error = target depth − measured depth
```

Positive error: it is too shallow, it needs to push down.

## P, I and D

The **PID** controller adds up three terms:

```
force = Kp × error + Ki × (sum of the error over time) − Kd × vertical velocity
```

- **P (proportional)**: pushes more the greater the error. On its own, it leaves a **steady-state error** when there is a constant force (the vehicle a bit light, for example): the equilibrium is where Kp × error = buoyancy balance.
- **I (integral)**: accumulates the error; while it exists, the force grows, until it **zeroes the steady-state error**. Too much integral causes oscillation.
- **D (derivative)**: reacts to the **velocity**: it brakes the vehicle when it approaches the target too fast, avoiding **overshoot**.

## Measuring quality

- **Overshoot**: how far it passed the target, as a % of the target.
- **Settling time**: from when it stays within ±2% of the target forever.
- **Steady-state error**: the difference left at the end.

## How to tune (practical recipe)

1. Start with **P** only and increase it until it responds quickly (it will oscillate or leave an error).
2. Add **D** until the oscillations disappear.
3. Add a little **I** to zero the final error; if it oscillates, reduce it.

## In the simulator

The ROV is **2 N lighter** than neutral (it tends to rise). The vertical thruster makes at most 20 N; the integral stops accumulating while the thruster is at its limit (anti-windup). Target: 10 m.
sub-09-controle-pid.task: With just a little P, the ROV stays still at ~9 m (steady-state error). Adjust **Kp**, **Ki** and **Kd** to reach **10 m ± 0.2 m**, with **overshoot ≤ 10%** and **settling within 60 s**.
hints: Increase Kp to respond faster, and Kd so it does not pass the target.
Without Ki the steady-state error never goes away: the 2 N balance has to be compensated by the integral.
Try something like Kp 20, Ki 1, Kd 80 and adjust from there.

questions.prompt: An ROV is **2 N** lighter than neutral and uses only **P** control with **Kp = 4 N/m**. How many metres above the target does it stay still?
questions.explanation: At equilibrium Kp × error = 2 N → error = 2 / 4 = 0.5 m.

questions.prompt: Which PID term eliminates the steady-state error?
questions.explanation: The integral grows as long as there is error, until the force compensates the imbalance.

questions.prompt: The ROV overshoots the target and keeps swinging. Which adjustment usually helps first?
questions.explanation: The D term reacts to velocity and damps the approach; more Ki or Kp usually make the oscillation worse.

sub-10-projeto-rov.title: Full project: the budget of an inspection ROV
sub-10-projeto-rov.theory:
# What is an ROV

An **ROV** (Remotely Operated Vehicle) is an underwater vehicle **piloted from the surface** through an **umbilical cable** (the tether), which carries power and data (video, commands). They are used to inspect oil platforms, ship hulls, dams, subsea cables, and for research.

## The design budget

As with rockets, engineering means closing several accounts at the same time:

- **Volume × mass** (buoyancy): the hull volume has to offset structure, electronics and payload (camera, lights, arm). Fine tuning with lead.
- **Stability**: lead in the keel, floats on top: positive BG.
- **Depth**: a hull with a safety factor ≥ 1.5 at the working depth.
- **Control**: a depth PID that is fast and without large overshoot (the pilot needs a stable image).
- **Power**: the thrusters have to overcome drag, and energy is limited.

## The cable is drag too

In a real ROV, the **cable** often has **more drag than the vehicle itself** in a current: hundreds of metres of 1 cm diameter cable have a lot of area. That is why thin, neutrally buoyant cables are used, and sometimes a "garage" (TMS) that descends close to the ROV.

## Energy

```
endurance (h) = battery energy (Wh) / average power (W)
```

An ROV powered through the cable does not have this limit, but the cable has to carry the power without heating up (that is why a higher voltage is used on the cable and converters in the vehicle).

## The mission

Inspect a pier at **40 m**, in the sea. The ROV has 18 kg of structure and electronics + 2.5 kg of camera and lights; the electronics sit a little above the centre of the hull. Define:

- the hull **volume** and **lead** (centre and keel) to be neutral and stable;
- the **hull strength** with a safety factor ≥ 1.5;
- the **vertical thruster and PID gains** to reach 40 m quickly and without overshooting much;
- the **shape and forward thruster** to go to and from the pier at ≥ 0.8 m/s using ≤ 40 W.
sub-10-projeto-rov.task: Close the inspection ROV's budget by meeting **all** the goals. Work in order: first buoyancy and stability, then the hull, then control, and finally propulsion.
sub-10-projeto-rov.safety:
- **Water and electricity**: use **low voltage** (12–48 V DC) in the vehicle and the cable; anything plugged into the mains stays away from the water and protected by a **residual-current device (RCD)**.
- Lithium batteries inside a hull need **protection (BMS)** and a relief valve: a battery that heats up in a sealed hull can generate gas and pressure.
- Never dive together with an ROV under test, and never operate near divers without coordination.
hints: In the sea, each litre of hull displaces 1.025 kg. To carry lead in the keel (stability), the hull needs extra volume: with ~24 L about ~4 kg of lead fit.
At 40 m in the sea the gauge pressure is ~4 bar. SF ≥ 1.5 → a hull of at least ~6 bar.
More force on the vertical thruster (30 N) makes the PID faster; use a high Kd so it does not pass the target.

questions.prompt: A **200 Wh** battery powers an ROV that consumes **80 W** on average. What is the endurance?
In a current, what usually has **more drag** on a deep inspection ROV?
options: The umbilical cable (hundreds of metres of area exposed to the current)
questions.explanation: Even thin, a long cable has an enormous area; that is why thin, neutrally buoyant cables and garages (TMS) are used.

questions.prompt: The ROV will work at **40 m in the sea** (gauge pressure ≈ 4.02 bar). What is the **minimum** hull strength for a safety factor of 1.5?

goals: CG at least 1 cm below the centre of buoyancy

sub-11-espuma-carga.title: Compensating payload with buoyancy foam
sub-11-espuma-carga.theory:
# New payload, new buoyancy

Every time an ROV gains a camera, a gripper or a sensor, it becomes **heavier without getting bigger** — and starts to sink. If there is no lead left to remove, the fix is to **add volume that weighs little**: a block of **buoyancy foam**.

## How much foam?

A block of volume V and density ρ_foam, under water, gives a **net** lift (buoyancy minus its own weight) of:

```
net lift = V × (ρ_water − ρ_foam) × g
```

To compensate a mass excess Δm:

```
V = Δm / (ρ_water − ρ_foam)
```

With **400 kg/m³** syntactic foam in fresh water, each litre holds up 0.6 kg; for 1 kg of excess you need **1.67 L**. In sea water (1025 kg/m³) 1.6 L is enough.

## Why syntactic foam?

Styrofoam and ordinary foams are full of air bubbles that **crush** under pressure: the volume (and the buoyancy) disappears with depth. **Syntactic foam** is made of **hollow glass microspheres** in a resin: it withstands hundreds or thousands of metres without changing volume.

## Where to put it

Foam goes **on top** (raises the centre of buoyancy) and ballast **at the bottom** (lowers the CG): this also improves stability, as in lesson 7.

## In this lab

The ROV (20 L, 18 kg) gained **3 kg** of camera and gripper. Adding foam increases the **volume** of the vehicle **and** its **mass** (0.4 kg per litre). Change both consistently.
sub-11-espuma-carga.task: With the 3 kg payload the ROV sinks. Add foam (400 kg/m³) by changing the **volume** and the **hull mass** consistently, until it is **neutral** (net force between −0.3 and +0.3 N) and holds still near **5 m**.
hints: The ROV is 1 kg heavier than the water it displaces (18 + 3 = 21 kg against 20 L).
1 kg / (1000 − 400) kg/m³ ≈ 1.7 L of foam, weighing 0.68 kg: volume 21.7 L and hull mass 18.7 kg.

questions.prompt: How many litres of **400 kg/m³** foam compensate **1 kg** of excess in **fresh water**?
And in **sea water** (1025 kg/m³)?
Why not use ordinary styrofoam as buoyancy on an ROV that dives to 500 m?
options: Because it dissolves in sea water
Because the air bubbles crush under pressure and the buoyancy disappears
questions.explanation: At 500 m the pressure is over 50 bar: closed-cell air foams shrink. Syntactic foam uses glass microspheres, which don't crush.

sub-12-velocidade-vertical.title: Going down calmly: vertical terminal speed
sub-12-velocidade-vertical.theory:
# Constant force, constant speed

A **neutral** ROV pushed down by a thruster with force F only accelerates at first. Soon the water **drag**, which grows with the square of the speed, matches the force — and the speed stops growing. That is the **terminal speed**:

```
F = ½ × ρ × Cd × A × v²   →   v = √(2F / (ρ × Cd × A))
```

Going down, the ROV "shows its belly" to the water: A is the side area (length × diameter) and Cd ≈ 1.1 (cylinder side-on).

## The square root is deceiving

Since v ∝ √F, to **double** the speed you need to **quadruple** the force. Conversely, a thruster 4 times weaker still goes down at half the speed.

## Why go down slowly

- Hitting the bottom fast stirs up sediment (the camera sees nothing anymore) and can damage the ROV or what is down there.
- The **umbilical cable** must be paid out at the pace of the descent.
- Human pilots have ascent limits (decompression); crewed vehicles go up and down a few metres per minute.

## Added mass

To accelerate a body in water you also have to accelerate part of the surrounding water — the **added mass** (for a cylinder side-on, ~ the mass of displaced water). That's why the ROV takes longer to reach terminal speed than in air.

## In this lab

A neutral 20 L ROV (cylinder ~16 cm × 97 cm, side area ≈ 0.157 m²), starting at 2 m, bottom at 30 m.
sub-12-velocidade-vertical.task: With 20 N downwards the ROV goes down at almost 0.5 m/s. Adjust the **vertical thruster** to go down **without exceeding 0.3 m/s** and still reach **at least 25 m** within the 2-minute dive.
hints: To drop from 0.48 to 0.3 m/s, the force has to drop by the ratio (0.3/0.48)² ≈ 0.39.
Too little force and the ROV doesn't reach 25 m in 120 s. Something between 5 and 7 N works.
goals: Peak vertical speed up to 0.3 m/s

questions.prompt: A neutral ROV is pushed down with **10 N**. With ρ = 1000 kg/m³, Cd = **1.1** and side area **0.16 m²**, what is the terminal speed?
With 10 N the ROV goes down at 0.34 m/s. What force would make it go down at **twice** that speed?
questions.explanation: F ∝ v²: doubling the speed takes 2² = 4 times the force: 40 N.

questions.prompt: Why does the ROV take longer to reach terminal speed in water than a similar object in air?
options: Because it also has to accelerate the surrounding water (added mass)
Because gravity is weaker under water
Because the thruster loses force in water
questions.explanation: The added mass (here, ~20 kg of water) adds to the ROV's when accelerating, so the same force gives less acceleration.

sub-13-espessura-casco.title: Sizing the hull: thickness, sphere and cylinder
sub-13-espessura-casco.theory:
# From pressure to thickness

For a thin-walled hull (radius r, thickness t) under pressure P, the wall stresses are:

```
cylinder (hoop stress):  σ = P × r / t
sphere:                  σ = P × r / (2t)
```

The **sphere** has half the stress of a cylinder with the same radius and thickness: it is the most efficient shape against pressure. That's why the cabin of deep submersibles is spherical.

## Designing the thickness

Inverting, with the **allowable stress** σ_allow (material strength divided by the safety factor):

```
cylinder:  t = P × r / σ_allow
sphere:    t = P × r / (2 σ_allow)
```

Example: at 6000 m in the sea, P ≈ 60 MPa. A titanium sphere of radius 1 m, with σ_allow = 900 MPa, needs t = 60 × 1 / 1800 ≈ **33 mm**.

## Design pressure

```
P = ρ × g × h        (gauge)
h = P / (ρ × g)      (depth for a given pressure)
```

60 MPa in the sea corresponds to 60 × 10⁶ / (1025 × 9.81) ≈ **5967 m**.

## Weight vs displacement

A thick hull is heavy. A submarine needs the **hull mass to be less than the mass of water it displaces** — otherwise it sinks even when empty. For great depths, this weight/displacement ratio gets worse fast, and materials with **high strength per density** (titanium, composites, ceramics) become essential.

## And buckling

The formulas above are for the material **yielding**. Thin hulls under **external** pressure usually fail earlier, by **buckling**: that's why there are stiffening rings and real tests in a pressure chamber.

questions.prompt: A titanium sphere of radius **1 m** must withstand **60 MPa** with an allowable stress of **900 MPa**. What is the minimum wall thickness? (t = P × r / (2σ))
At what depth in the **sea** (ρ = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²) does the gauge pressure reach **60 MPa**?
An aluminium tube of radius **0.1 m** must withstand **1 MPa** (~100 m). Aluminium resists 250 MPa and the safety factor is **2**. What is the minimum thickness by hoop stress?
questions.explanation: σ_allow = 250 / 2 = 125 MPa. t = 1 × 0.1 / 125 = 0.0008 m = 0.8 mm — and, in practice, much thicker because of buckling.

questions.prompt: With the same radius, thickness and pressure, the wall stress of a **sphere** compared with a **cylinder** is…
questions.explanation: σ_sphere = P r / (2t) and σ_cylinder = P r / t: the sphere splits the load in two directions.

questions.prompt: Why are materials with **high strength per density** essential for very deep vehicles?
options: Because the thick hull must still be lighter than the water it displaces
questions.explanation: Thickness grows with pressure; if the hull becomes heavier than its displacement, the vehicle sinks even when empty.

sub-14-sonar.title: Sonar: seeing with sound
sub-14-sonar.theory:
# Sound is the ocean's light

Light and radio waves vanish in a few metres of water; **sound** travels kilometres, at ~**1500 m/s** (over 4 times faster than in air). That's why navigation, mapping and communication under water use **sonar** (SOund NAvigation and Ranging).

## Active and passive

- **Active**: sends a pulse ("ping") and measures the **echo time**. The distance is **c × t / 2** (there and back).
- **Passive**: only listens (propellers, machinery, animals). It doesn't give away the listener — the preferred mode of military submarines.

## Frequency: range vs detail

The wavelength is λ = c / f. **High frequencies** (hundreds of kHz) have millimetre wavelengths: detailed images, but a range of tens of metres (water absorbs more). **Low frequencies** (a few kHz) reach tens of km, with little resolution.

## Losses along the way

Sound spreads as a sphere: intensity falls with 1/R², which in decibels is a loss of **20 log₁₀(R)** (60 dB at 1000 m). Add to that **absorption**, which grows with frequency.

## Doppler effect

If the target (or the ROV) moves with speed v towards the sonar, the echo comes back with its frequency shifted by:

```
Δf ≈ 2 × v × f / c
```

That's how a **DVL** (Doppler Velocity Log) measures the ROV's speed over the seabed.

## Layers and shadow zones

The speed of sound changes with temperature, salinity and pressure. The **thermocline** bends sound rays and creates **shadow zones** where a submarine can hide.

questions.prompt: A sonar ping's echo comes back **0.8 s** later. With sound at **1500 m/s**, how far is the target?
questions.explanation: d = 1500 × 0.8 / 2 = 600 m (the sound goes there and back).

questions.prompt: What is the wavelength of a **200 kHz** imaging sonar in water (c = 1500 m/s)?
questions.explanation: λ = 1500 / 200 000 = 0.0075 m = 7.5 mm: centimetre-level detail, short range.

questions.prompt: An ROV approaches a target at **5 m/s** using a **10 kHz** sonar. What is the Doppler shift of the echo? (Δf ≈ 2vf/c, c = 1500 m/s)
How much does sound lose by spherical spreading over **1000 m**? (loss = 20 log₁₀ R)
questions.explanation: 20 × log₁₀(1000) = 20 × 3 = 60 dB (one way only; the echo loses it again on the way back).

questions.prompt: Why does a military submarine prefer **passive** sonar?
options: Because sending a ping reveals its own position
Because passive always has more range
Because active doesn't work in the sea
Because passive measures distance more precisely
questions.explanation: A ping can be heard very far away — farther than its own echo returns. Listening in silence gives nothing away.

sub-15-energia-autonomia.title: Energy and endurance: the maximum-range speed
sub-15-energia-autonomia.theory:
# Where the battery goes

The power of an electric underwater vehicle has two parts:

- **Hotel load** H: electronics, cameras, lights, sensors, heating — it costs the same **standing still or moving**.
- **Propulsion**: overcomes drag. Since drag ∝ v² and power = drag × v, propulsion grows with **v³**:

```
P(v) = H + k × v³
endurance (h) = E / P(v)
range = v × endurance = E × v / (H + k v³)
```

## Too slow, too fast

- **Too slow**: propulsion is small, but the hotel keeps draining for hours — and the vehicle barely moves.
- **Too fast**: propulsion (v³) dominates and the battery runs out early.

**Maximum range** happens when propulsion uses **half** of the hotel load:

```
k v³ = H / 2   →   v_best = ∛(H / (2k))
```

## Example

An AUV with a **2 kWh** battery, **50 W** hotel and **150 W of propulsion at 1 m/s** (k = 150 W/(m/s)³):

- at 1 m/s: P = 200 W → 10 h → **36 km**;
- at 2 m/s: P = 50 + 1200 = 1250 W → 1.6 h → **11.5 km**;
- v_best = ∛(50/300) ≈ **0.55 m/s**.

## Energy sources

AUVs use **lithium-ion** (~150–250 Wh/kg); military submarines use **diesel-electric** (they must come up to breathe through the snorkel), **AIP** (air-independent propulsion, weeks submerged) or a **nuclear reactor** (months, limited by the crew's food).

questions.prompt: A **2 kWh** battery, **50 W** hotel and **150 W** of propulsion at 1 m/s. What is the endurance at 1 m/s?
What is the range at that speed (1 m/s)?
And the range at **2 m/s**? (propulsion grows with v³)
What is this AUV's **maximum-range** speed? (v = ∛(H / (2k)), k = 150 W/(m/s)³)
questions.explanation: v = ∛(50 / 300) = ∛0.1667 ≈ 0.55 m/s. At it, the range goes above 42 km.

questions.prompt: If the AUV gets cameras and lights that **increase the hotel load**, the maximum-range speed…
options: Increases: it's worth going faster to spend less time
questions.explanation: v_best = ∛(H/2k) grows with H: if standing still is expensive, it pays to get there sooner.

sub-16-pid-saturacao.title: PID with a heavy ROV: saturation and anti-windup
sub-16-pid-saturacao.theory:
# When the thruster can't keep up

In lesson 9 the ROV was nearly neutral. Now it carries **2 kg** of tools: it is **19.6 N heavier** than neutral, and the vertical thruster has only **30 N**. Two things change:

## 1. The P controller's error becomes large

With P only, the ROV stops where the controller's force balances the extra weight:

```
error = ΔF / Kp = 19.6 / Kp
```

With Kp = 5 N/m, that's ~4 m of error (it sits **below** the target). The **I** term accumulates that error and ends up supplying the 19.6 N on its own.

## 2. Saturation

The controller may ask for 100 N, but the thruster delivers 30 N at most: the output **saturates**. Worse: of those 30 N, 19.6 N already go just to holding the weight — there's little left to **climb**, and plenty to **descend** (gravity helps). The response becomes **asymmetric**.

## Integrator wind-up

During saturation the error stays large and the integrator **keeps accumulating**. When the ROV finally reaches the target, the "full" integrator pushes too hard and causes a huge overshoot. The defence is **anti-windup**: freeze the integral while the output is saturated (the simulator already does this).

## Tuning recipe

1. Generous Kd for damping (water dissipates little in the vertical).
2. Kp until the response is fast without oscillating.
3. Small Ki, only to remove the final error — too big a Ki brings back oscillation.

## In this lab

A 20 L ROV with 2 kg of payload, 30 N thruster, target at **25 m**, a 3-minute dive.
sub-16-pid-saturacao.task: Tune the PID so the heavy ROV stops **between 24.5 and 25.5 m**, with an overshoot of **up to 5%** and settling within **70 s**.
hints: Start with a high Kd (100 or more) and raise Kp until the descent is firm.
P alone leaves the ROV below the target. A Ki of ~1 removes that error without upsetting the rest.

questions.prompt: The ROV is **2 kg** heavier than neutral and uses only **P** with **Kp = 30 N/m**. How many metres below the target does it stop? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
The thruster gives at most **30 N** and the ROV is **19.62 N** heavier than neutral. How much **upward** force is left to make it climb?
questions.explanation: 30 − 19.62 = 10.38 N. To descend, on the other hand, there's 30 + 19.62 ≈ 49.6 N: the response is asymmetric.

questions.prompt: What is integrator **wind-up**?
options: The integrator resets itself when the error is small
The motor overheats from using the I term a lot
With the output saturated, the integral keeps growing and later causes a large overshoot
The D term amplifies sensor noise
questions.explanation: While the actuator is at its limit, accumulating error does nothing useful — it only stores a "push" that comes out at the wrong time. Anti-windup freezes the integral during that period.

sub-17-mergulho-profundo.title: Deep dive: ballast, timing and safety factor
sub-17-mergulho-profundo.theory:
# Down to the bottom and back

A ballast vehicle (no vertical thruster) does a deep mission like this:

1. **Floods the tank**: becomes heavy and sinks at terminal speed.
2. Reaches the bottom and works.
3. **Blows the tank** with compressed air: becomes light and rises.

The pilot has to decide **when** to blow: too early, it doesn't reach the bottom; too late, the battery or the time runs out.

## Descent time

```
time ≈ depth / terminal speed
```

At 0.42 m/s, 90 m take ~214 s (plus a little to accelerate).

## Hull safety factor

The pressure at 90 m in the sea is P = 1025 × 9.81 × 90 ≈ **9.05 bar** (gauge). A hull that withstands exactly that is at its limit: any flaw, fatigue or measurement error and it implodes. Serious designs use a **safety factor** of 1.5 or more:

```
required rating = SF × ρ × g × h_max
```

For 90 m and SF = 1.5: **13.6 bar**.

## Compressed air at depth

To push the water out of the tank, the air must be above the outside pressure — at 90 m, over 10 bar absolute. The deeper, the more air (and more bottles) each blow uses.

## In this lab

A 20 L, 19 kg vehicle, full 3 L tank, **sea water**, bottom at **90 m**, 500 s mission.
sub-17-mergulho-profundo.task: Make the vehicle **touch the bottom** (at least 89 m), **return to the surface** before the mission ends, and dive with a **safety factor of at least 1.5** — without imploding. Choose the **hull rating** and **when to blow the ballast**.
sub-17-mergulho-profundo.safety:
- Real deep dives require a hull **tested in a pressure chamber** above the working pressure, with third-party certification.
- Pressure tests of amateur projects: **with water** (never air), behind protection, with nobody in front of viewports and end caps.
hints: The descent takes about 220 s. Blowing before that leaves the vehicle far from the bottom.
1.5 × 9.05 bar ≈ 13.6 bar: pick a rating a bit above that.
goals: Hull safety factor of at least 1.5

questions.prompt: What is the **gauge** pressure at **90 m** in the sea? (ρ = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)
What minimum rating does the hull need to go to 90 m with a **safety factor of 1.5**?
Going down at a constant **0.42 m/s**, how long does the vehicle take to reach **90 m**?
questions.explanation: t = 90 / 0.42 ≈ 214 s — that's why blowing the ballast before ~220 s won't let it reach the bottom.

sub-18-hidrodinamica.title: Hydrodynamics: Reynolds, power and cavitation
sub-18-hidrodinamica.theory:
# The Reynolds number

How the flow behaves around a hull depends on the ratio between **inertial** and **viscous** forces:

```
Re = v × L / ν
```

(v: speed; L: length; ν: kinematic viscosity, ~1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s for water at 20 °C). Below ~5 × 10⁵ the boundary layer tends to be **laminar**; above, **turbulent** (more friction, but separates less). A 1 m ROV at 2 m/s has Re = 2 × 10⁶: turbulent.

## Drag and power

```
D = ½ × ρ × Cd × A × v²
P = D × v = ½ × ρ × Cd × A × v³
```

A hull with Cd = 0.1 and A = 0.03 m², at 3 m/s in the sea, needs ½ × 1025 × 0.1 × 0.03 × 27 ≈ **41.5 W** of useful power.

## Shapes that slip through

The **teardrop/torpedo** shape (rounded nose, slowly tapering tail) avoids flow separation at the back — the **pressure** drag almost vanishes and only **friction** drag remains. The best length/diameter ratio is around 6–8.

## Cavitation

On the blades of a fast propeller the local pressure can drop below the water's **vapour pressure**: bubbles form and implode, making **noise** (the enemy of a quiet submarine), eroding the metal and stealing thrust. Cavitation appears more **near the surface** (less pressure) and on **fast propellers**; at depth, the higher pressure suppresses it.

## Free surface

Near the surface, the hull makes **waves**, which cost energy (wave resistance). That's why submarines are faster **submerged** than on the surface.

questions.prompt: What is the Reynolds number of a **1 m** long ROV at **2 m/s** (ν = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s)?
questions.explanation: Re = 2 × 1 / 10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁶ — turbulent flow.

questions.prompt: What useful power overcomes the drag of a hull with Cd = **0.1** and A = **0.03 m²** at **3 m/s** in the sea (ρ = 1025 kg/m³)?
If the speed **doubles**, the power to overcome drag is multiplied by how much?
questions.explanation: P ∝ v³: 2³ = 8.

questions.prompt: Where is a propeller **more** likely to cavitate?
questions.explanation: Cavitation = local pressure below the vapour pressure. Low ambient pressure (surface) and fast blades (big pressure drop) favour it.

questions.prompt: Why is a submarine usually **faster submerged** than on the surface?
options: Because submerged it spends no energy making waves
Because deep water is less dense
Because the engine works better under pressure
questions.explanation: On the surface part of the power becomes waves (wave resistance). Well below the surface, only friction and form drag remain.

sub-19-fadiga-seguranca.title: Fatigue, certification and lessons from real accidents
sub-19-fadiga-seguranca.theory:
# A hull doesn't fail only from too much pressure

A hull can withstand the maximum pressure on the first dive and fail on the tenth. Each descent and ascent is a **load cycle**; micro-cracks grow a little each cycle — that is **fatigue**.

## Miner's rule

If a material withstands N₁ cycles at a certain load, each cycle "uses up" 1/N₁ of its life. Adding up the fractions of several kinds of dive:

```
D = n₁/N₁ + n₂/N₂ + ...
```

When D reaches 1, failure is expected. In practice the hull is retired well before (D ≈ 0.3–0.5), because the scatter is large.

## Design and test pressure

At 4000 m in the sea the pressure is 1025 × 9.81 × 4000 ≈ **40.2 MPa**. With a safety factor of 1.5, the hull is designed for **60.3 MPa**, and classification society rules (DNV, ABS, Lloyd's) require **pressure-chamber testing** above the working pressure, periodic inspection and material traceability.

## Composites and monitoring

Metals give warning: they deform and crack detectably. **Carbon-fibre composites** under cyclic compression can build up **internal** damage (delamination) invisible from outside. Acoustic sensors that "hear" fibres snapping help, but they **don't replace** a validated, certified design.

## The Titan case (2023)

The Titan submersible imploded on its way to the Titanic (~3800 m). Investigations pointed to: a **carbon-fibre** cylindrical hull (a poor material for cyclic compression), earlier signs of damage after dives, **no independent certification** and internal warnings ignored. The engineering lesson: **margin, testing, certification and a safety culture** are not red tape.

questions.prompt: What is the gauge pressure at **4000 m** in the sea? (ρ = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)
With a **safety factor of 1.5**, what pressure should the hull be designed for?
A hull made **50** dives of a kind it could withstand **200** times and **30** of another kind it could withstand **100** times. What is the accumulated damage D by Miner's rule?
questions.explanation: D = 50/200 + 30/100 = 0.25 + 0.30 = 0.55: more than half of the estimated life is already used up.

questions.prompt: Why are **carbon-fibre** hulls under repeated compression especially dangerous?
options: Because internal damage (delamination) grows without showing outside
Because they can't take even one dive
questions.explanation: The composite may pass the first dives and build up hidden damage; metals usually give visible signs first.

questions.prompt: Which of these practices is the **most** important for a crewed submersible?
options: A design with margin, testing above working pressure and independent certification
Make many dives to "break in" the hull
questions.explanation: Monitoring helps, but doesn't replace design margin, testing and independent verification — the main lesson of accidents like Titan.

sub-20-projeto-auv.title: Final project: a sea inspection AUV
sub-20-projeto-auv.theory:
# Every requirement at once

An **AUV** (autonomous vehicle) will inspect a pipeline at **60 m** in the sea. It carries **3 kg** of sensors mounted **on top** of the hull (the CG of the fixed part is 0.5 cm above the centre of buoyancy). The requirements come from every lesson of this track:

1. **Buoyancy**: nearly neutral in sea water (net force between −1 and +1 N). Lead at the centre does the fine trim.
2. **Stability**: CG at least **0.5 cm below** the centre of buoyancy — lead in the **keel**. But lead is heavy: to stay neutral you need **more volume**.
3. **Hull**: no implosion and a **safety factor ≥ 1.5** at 60 m.
4. **Control**: PID reaching 60 m within 150 s, with up to 5% overshoot.
5. **Propulsion**: cruise at least **2 m/s** using **up to 40 W** — shape and thruster force.

## An order that works

1. Work out how much keel lead gives BG ≥ 0.5 cm (the moment of the lead down low must beat that of the payload up high).
2. Increase the volume until buoyancy covers hull + payload + lead; trim the rest with the centre lead.
3. Choose the hull rating: 1.5 × 1025 × 9.81 × 60 ≈ 9 bar, with some margin.
4. Tune the PID (high Kd, then Kp, small Ki).
5. Choose the shape and reduce the forward thruster until the power fits the budget.

## Endurance

With a 500 Wh battery, 30 W of propulsion and 20 W of hotel load, the AUV runs for 10 h — at 2 m/s, **72 km** of pipeline inspected.
sub-20-projeto-auv.task: Close the design: **neutral** (−1 to +1 N), **BG ≥ 0.5 cm**, no implosion and **safety factor ≥ 1.5**, PID settling within **150 s** with overshoot **up to 5%**, cruise **≥ 2 m/s** using **up to 40 W**.
hints: About 3.6 kg of keel lead gives BG ≈ 0.6 cm. Then there are 30 + 3.6 = 33.6 kg to hold up: a 33 L hull and about 200 g at the centre.
A torpedo with ~6 N of forward thrust passes 2 m/s using ~30 W. For the PID, try Kp 30, Ki 1 and Kd 120 with a 30 N vertical thruster.
goals: CG at least 0.5 cm below the centre of buoyancy

questions.explanation: Displaced water = 33 × 1.025 = 33.825 kg. Lead = 33.825 − 30 = 3.825 kg (keel + centre).
